clinicalPearls: Anorchia is the absence of testicular tissue in a phenotypically male, 46,XY individual, and may be unilateral or bilateral
It is thought to result from a vanishing testis, in which a testis that was present and functional early in fetal life later regresses, often from an intrauterine vascular or torsion event
Because early testicular function drove normal male differentiation, the external genitalia and Wolffian structures are typically male, distinguishing it from disorders of sex development
In bilateral anorchia the child presents with an empty scrotum and impalpable testes, and the key task is to distinguish absent testes from bilateral intra-abdominal cryptorchidism

Hormonal assessment is central: markedly raised gonadotropins with very low or absent inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone, and no rise in testosterone after hCG stimulation, support absent functional testicular tissue
The hCG stimulation test and measurement of inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone help confirm anorchia, but laparoscopy is often required to be certain no intra-abdominal testis or nubbin is present
Management includes androgen replacement to induce and maintain puberty in bilateral cases, consideration of a testicular prosthesis, and psychological support and counselling
reference.pathophysiology: In congenital anorchia the testis develops and functions early enough in fetal life to drive male differentiation of the genital tract and external genitalia, but subsequently undergoes regression, most likely from an intrauterine vascular accident or perinatal torsion, leaving little or no identifiable testicular tissue, sometimes only a fibrous nubbin with haemosiderin and calcification. The loss of functioning Sertoli and Leydig cells removes the sources of inhibin B, anti-Mullerian hormone, and testosterone, so gonadotropins rise while these markers fall, and there is no testosterone response to hCG stimulation. In bilateral disease this produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism requiring lifelong androgen replacement.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral intra-abdominal cryptorchidism (undescended but present testes)
Disorders of sex development with dysgenetic gonads
Testicular regression with a residual nubbin
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low rather than high gonadotropins)
additionalInvestigations: Serum FSH and LH (typically markedly elevated in bilateral anorchia)
Inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone as markers of Sertoli cell tissue
hCG stimulation test to assess for any testosterone-producing tissue
Karyotype to confirm 46,XY and exclude a disorder of sex development
Scrotal and abdominal ultrasound or MRI to search for testicular tissue
Diagnostic laparoscopy to confirm absence of an intra-abdominal testis or locate a nubbin
redFlags: Bilateral impalpable testes requiring urgent distinction from intra-abdominal testes at risk of malignancy
Ambiguous genitalia or atypical phenotype suggesting a disorder of sex development
Failure to enter or progress through puberty without treatment
An intra-abdominal testicular remnant that may need removal because of malignant potential
reference.prognosis: With appropriate androgen replacement, boys with bilateral anorchia can undergo normal virilisation and pubertal development and maintain secondary sexual characteristics and bone health, though natural fertility is not possible; unilateral anorchia with a normal solitary testis usually allows normal development and fertility.
pitfalls: Assuming impalpable testes are absent without excluding intra-abdominal cryptorchidism
Relying on imaging alone when laparoscopy is often needed to confirm absent testes
Overlooking the malignant potential of an intra-abdominal remnant or undescended testis
Delaying androgen replacement and prosthesis discussion, with psychological consequences
Mislabelling a disorder of sex development as simple anorchia without a karyotype
management: Provide androgen (testosterone) replacement in bilateral anorchia to induce and maintain virilisation, pubertal development, and secondary sexual characteristics
Safeguard bone health through adequate androgenisation, calcium and vitamin D, and monitoring of bone density
Confirm the diagnosis and exclude an intra-abdominal testis by laparoscopy, removing any dysgenetic nubbin to eliminate malignancy risk
Offer a testicular prosthesis for cosmetic and psychological benefit
Provide psychological support and fertility counselling, since natural fertility is not possible, and discuss donor options
Monitor growth and pubertal progression through adolescence under endocrine follow-up
In unilateral anorchia, protect and monitor the function of the solitary testis
